source_text: Si quid retro gestum est nobis aduersus Marcionem. iam hinc uiderit. nouam rem adgredimur ex uetere. primum opusculum quasi properatum pleniore postea compositione rescideram. hanc quoque nondum exemplariis suffectam fraude tunc fratris, dehinc apostatae, amisi, qui forte descripserat quaedam mendosissime et exhibuit frequentiae. emendationis necessitas facta est innouationis. eius occasio aliquid adicere persuasit. ita stilus iste nunc de secundo tertius et de tertio iam hinc primus hunc opusculi sui exitum necessario praefatur, ne quem uarietas eius in disperso reperta confundat. Pontus igitur, qui Euxinus natura negatur, nomine inluditur. ceterum hospitalem Pontum nec de situ aestimes; ita ab humanioribus fretis nostris quasi quodam barbariae suae pudore secessit. gentes ferocissimae inhabitant; si tamen habitatur in plaustro. sedes incerta, uita cruda, libido promiscua et plurimum nuda; etiam cum abscondunt, suspensis de iugo pharetris ut indicibus notantur, ne qui intercedat. ita nec armis suis erubescunt. parentum cadauera cum pecudibus caesa conuiuio conuorant. qui non ita decesserint, ut escatiles iuerint, maledicta mors est. nec feminae sexu mitigantur secundum pudorem; ubera excludunt, pensum securibus faciunt, malunt militare quam nubere. duritia de caelo quoque. dies numquam patens, sol numquam ridens, unus aer nebula, totus annus hibernum, omne quod fiauerit aquilo est. liquores niuibus redeunt, amnes glacie negantur, montes pruina exaggerantur. omnia torpent, omnia rigent; nihil illic nisi feritas calet, illa scilicet, quae fabulas scaenis dedit de sacrificiis Taurorum et amoribus Colchorum et crucibus Caucasorum. sed nihil tam barbarum ac triste apud Pontum quam quod illic Marcion natus est, Scytha tetrior, Hamaxobio instabilior, Massageta inhumanior, Amazona audacior, nubilo obscurior, hieme frigidior, gelu fragilior, Histro fallacior, Caucaso abruptior. quidni? penes quem uerus Prometheus, deus omnipotens, blasphemiis lancinatur. iam et bestiis illius barbariei importunior Marcion. quis enim tam castrator carnis castor quam qui nuptias abstulit? quis tam comesor mus Ponticus quam qui euangelia conrosit? ne tu, Euxine, probabiliorem feram philosophis edidisti quam Christianis. nam ille canicola Diogenes hominem inuenire cupiebat. lucernam meridie circumferens, Marcion deum, quem inuenerat, extincto lumine fidei suae amisit. non negabunt discipuli eius primam illius fidem nobiscum fuisse, ipsius litteris testibus, ut hinc iam destinari possit haereticus qui deserto quod prius fuerat id postea sibi elegerit, quod retro non erat. in tantum enim haeresis deputabitur quod postea inducitur, in quantum ueritas habebitur quod retro et a primordio traditum est. sed alius libellus hunc gradum sustinebit aduersus haereticos, etiam sine retractatu doctrinarum reuincendos. quod hoc sint de praescriptione nouitatis. nunc quatenus admittenda congressio est interdum, ne compendium praescriptionis ubique aduocatum diffidentiae deputetur, regulam prius aduersarii praetexam, ne cui lateat, in qua principalis quaestio dimicatura est.
thought_title: Introduction to the Argument Against Marcion
pass_a_gloss: If something was done previously by us against Marcion, let it be seen from here. We are undertaking a new matter from an old one. At first, I had rescinded a hasty little work with a fuller composition later. I also lost this one, not yet supplied with copies, through the fraud of a brother, then an apostate, who perhaps had written down certain things very incorrectly and presented them to the public. The necessity of correction became an opportunity for innovation. This occasion has persuaded me to add something. Thus, this style, now third and from the second, and from the third now first, necessarily prefaces the outcome of this little work, so that the variety of it, found scattered, may not confuse anyone. Therefore, Pontus, which is denied by nature to be the Euxine, is mocked by its name. However, you should not judge the hospitable Pontus by its location; it has withdrawn from our more humane shores, as if in shame of its own barbarity. The most ferocious nations inhabit it; if, indeed, it is inhabited in a wagon. The dwelling is uncertain, life is crude, and lust is promiscuous and mostly naked; even when they hide, they are marked by suspended quivers on their yoke, so that no one may intervene. Thus, they do not blush at their own arms. They devour the corpses of their parents with slaughtered animals at a feast. Death is cursed if they did not die in such a way that they were eaten. Women are not softened by their sex according to modesty; they exclude their breasts, make a burden for their axes, and prefer to wage war rather than marry. The harshness is also from heaven; the day is never open, the sun never smiles, the air is one cloud, the whole year is winter, and everything that blows is the north wind. Liquids return with snow, rivers are denied by ice, and mountains are heaped up with frost. Everything is numb, everything is stiff; nothing there is warm except savagery, that is, the savagery that gave stories to the stages about the sacrifices of the Tauri and the loves of the Colchi and the crosses of the Caucasians. But nothing is as barbarous and sad in Pontus as the fact that Marcion was born there, worse than a Scythian, more unstable than a Hamaxobian, more inhuman than a Massagete, more daring than an Amazon, darker than a cloud, colder than winter, more fragile than frost, more deceitful than the Hister, and more abrupt than the Caucasus. Why not? For with him, the true Prometheus, the all-powerful God, is torn apart by blasphemies. Now Marcion is even more troublesome to the beasts of that barbarity. For who is as much a castrator of flesh as he who took away marriages? Who is as much a devourer of the Pontic mouse as he who gnawed away the Gospels? Have you, Euxine, produced a more probable beast for philosophers than for Christians? For that cynic Diogenes sought to find a human being, carrying a lantern in the daytime. Marcion, having found God, lost Him with the extinguished light of his faith. His disciples will not deny that his first faith was with us, as his letters testify, so that from here it can already be determined that a heretic is one who, having deserted what he previously was, later chooses for himself what he was not before. For to such an extent will heresy be reckoned as what is introduced later, inasmuch as the truth will be held to be what was handed down before and from the beginning. But another little book will sustain this level against the heretics, even without a re-examination of doctrines, to be overcome. This is what they know about the prescription of novelty. Now, insofar as a confrontation is to be admitted from time to time, lest the summary of the prescription be deemed everywhere to be advocated by diffidence, I will first weave the rule of the adversary, lest it be hidden from anyone, in which the principal question will be fought.

pass_b_english: If we have done anything against Marcion before, let the record show it from this point on. We are launching a new work from an old foundation. I first withdrew a hasty little treatise, later replacing it with a fuller composition. I lost that one too, before it could be copied, thanks to the fraud of a brother who then turned apostate — he had copied certain passages very badly and circulated them publicly. The need for correction became an opportunity for innovation, and that occasion persuaded me to add more. So this pen, now third after the second, and now first after the third, must preface the outcome of this little work, so that its scattered variety may not confuse anyone.

Pontus, denied by nature the name Euxine, is mocked by it instead. But do not judge hospitable Pontus by its location; it has withdrawn from our more humane shores as if in shame of its own barbarity. The most ferocious nations inhabit it — if you can call it inhabited, given they live in wagons. Their dwellings are uncertain, life is crude, lust promiscuous and mostly naked; even when they hide, they are marked by quivers suspended from their yokes, so that no one may intervene. Thus they do not blush at their own arms. They devour the corpses of their parents alongside slaughtered beasts at a feast. Death is cursed if they do not die so as to be eaten. Women are not softened by their sex according to modesty; they bind their breasts, make a burden for their axes, and prefer to wage war rather than marry.

Harshness comes from heaven as well: the day is never open, the sun never smiles, the air is one unbroken cloud, the whole year is winter, and everything that blows is the north wind. Liquids freeze back into snow, rivers are stopped by ice, mountains are heaped with frost. Everything is numb, everything stiff; nothing there is warm except savagery — the savagery that gave the stage its stories of Tauric sacrifices, Colchian loves, and Caucasian crosses. But nothing in Pontus is as barbarous and sad as the fact that Marcion was born there: worse than a Scythian, more unstable than a Hamaxobian, more inhuman than a Massagete, more daring than an Amazon, darker than a cloud, colder than winter, more fragile than frost, more deceitful than the Hister, more abrupt than the Caucasus. Why not? For with him the true Prometheus, God Almighty, is torn apart by blasphemies.

Now Marcion is even more troublesome to the beasts of that barbarity. For who is as much a castrator of flesh as the man who abolished marriage? Who is as much a devourer of the Pontic mouse as the man who gnawed away the Gospels? Did you, Euxine, produce a more probable beast for philosophers than for Christians? That cynic Diogenes sought to find a human being, carrying a lantern at midday. Marcion, having found God, lost Him with the extinguished light of his faith.

His disciples will not deny that his first faith was with us, as his own letters testify, so that from this point it can already be determined: a heretic is one who, having deserted what he previously was, later chooses for himself what he was not before. For to such an extent will heresy be reckoned as what is introduced later, inasmuch as truth will be held to be what was handed down before and from the beginning.

But another little book will sustain this level against the heretics, even without a re-examination of doctrines, to be overcome. This is what they know about the prescription of novelty. Now, insofar as a confrontation is to be admitted from time to time, lest the summary of the prescription be deemed everywhere to be advocated out of diffidence, I will first weave the rule of the adversary, lest it be hidden from anyone, in which the principal question will be fought.

review.notes: The translation accurately captures the complex Latin syntax and the polemical tone of the source. All clauses, including the lengthy list of comparisons for Marcion and the description of the Pontic landscape, are preserved in both Pass A and Pass B. The distinction between the 'new' work and the 'old' one is maintained. The theological definition of heresy (that which is introduced later vs. truth handed down from the beginning) is correctly rendered. No omissions or additions were noted.
